campbell-diagram.summary: Follow how vibration frequencies and amplitudes change as a shaft speeds up.
campbell-diagram.useWhen: Compare bearing run-ups, track harmonics tied to shaft rotation, or find speeds where vibration strengthens at a particular frequency.
campbell-diagram.data: Supply at least two nonnegative frequencies in Hz in strictly increasing order. Each run needs a unique id, a label, at least two nonnegative shaft speeds in RPM in strictly increasing order, and one spectrum of finite amplitudes per speed. The amplitude at speed index i and frequency index j is levelsDb[i][j].
campbell-diagram.reading: The heatmap shows shaft speed in RPM along the horizontal axis and vibration frequency in Hz along the vertical axis. Both bearing runs share the shaft speed, frequency, and relative amplitude scales. Areas outside the selected run’s measured speed range are blank. Select a shaft speed to inspect its complete spectrum.
notes: The measured example compares two University of Ottawa run-ups, a healthy bearing (H-A-1) and a bearing with an inner-race fault (I-A-1). The healthy run spans 862–1,420 RPM and the fault run spans 759–1,638 RPM.

Each run supplies 40 nonoverlapping 250 ms windows of 200 kHz accelerometer data. Each window is demeaned and Hann tapered before computing the FFT. The chart shows 100 frequency bins from 4 to 400 Hz. Speed is estimated from encoder pulse timing within each window.

The strongest amplitude across both runs and the displayed frequency band is the common 0 dB reference. For an amplitude spectrum, use 20 × log₁₀(amplitude / reference amplitude) and apply the same floor across runs.

The diagonal lines mark shaft orders. Order n occurs at n × RPM / 60 Hz. A ridge that follows an order tracks shaft rotation. A ridge that remains at the same frequency as speed changes can indicate a structural mode.
The heatmap interpolates between sample centers. The readout and spectrum show original bin values. Keep the windowing, frequency bins, and amplitude reference consistent when comparing runs.

mode-shapes.summary: See how a cantilever beam bends in each of its first four natural modes.
mode-shapes.useWhen: Compare bending patterns, locate vibration nodes, or connect a natural frequency to the shape of the corresponding motion.
mode-shapes.data: Supply a uniform rectangular beam with length, width, and thickness in metres, Young’s modulus in pascals, and density in kilograms per cubic metre. All values must be positive and finite. The example computes Euler–Bernoulli modes for a 600 × 30 × 3 mm steel strip with a modulus of 200 GPa and a density of 7,850 kg/m³.
mode-shapes.reading: Choose mode 1–4 to see its calculated natural frequency in Hz. The horizontal axis shows normalized span x/L, from 0 at the clamp to 1 at the free tip. The vertical axis shows normalized transverse deflection u/A₀ on a fixed scale shared by all four modes.
notes: The model computes free, undamped bending in the thickness direction. The clamp holds both displacement and slope at zero. The free end has zero bending moment and shear force.

The displayed deflection is u/A₀ = (s/100) cos(θ) φₙ(x)/φₙ(L). Here s is the deformation scale from 25% to 150%, θ is the phase, φₙ is the mode shape, and A₀ is an arbitrary reference tip amplitude at 100% scale.
Dashed curves mark the phase limits at 0° and 180° for the selected deformation scale. Hollow circles mark interior nodes, which stay at zero transverse deflection throughout the cycle.

Set the phase to 0°, 90°, 180°, or 270° for quarter-cycle snapshots. Playback shows one cycle in about 2.4 seconds for every mode. The modeled oscillation period in seconds is the reciprocal of the displayed natural frequency in Hz.
The example predicts frequencies of 6.79, 42.58, 119.23, and 233.65 Hz. The model assumes a slender beam with small deflections and an ideal clamp.
For this rectangular section, width cancels out of the ratio of bending stiffness to mass per unit length. Increasing thickness raises the natural frequencies, and increasing length lowers them.

shaft-orbit.summary: Follow the motion of a rotating shaft in two perpendicular probe signals.
shaft-orbit.useWhen: Compare the shape of an orbit across test runs, or check which part of each probe waveform produces a loop or turn in the path.
shaft-orbit.data: Give each run a unique ID, a label, a positive sample rate in Hz, and equal-length X and Y arrays of finite displacement values in µm. Both channels must share a sampling clock. Supply at least two strictly increasing, zero-based integer trigger indices inside the arrays. Each trigger marks the same shaft angle one revolution apart.
shaft-orbit.reading: Select a run and a revolution, then move the phase control. In the orbit, X displacement is horizontal and Y displacement is vertical. Both axes use equal physical scales in µm and the same limits across runs. The paired waveforms show X as a solid line and Y as a dashed line on the same time grid, in milliseconds from the trigger.
notes: The three simulated runs span 12 revolutions at 1,800 RPM (30 Hz), sampled at 5,760 Hz. The first shows a 30 Hz ellipse. The other two add a 60 Hz second harmonic (2×) or a 13.8 Hz subsynchronous component (0.46×). That lower-frequency component changes the orbit between turns.
Each simulated channel is centered by subtracting its mean over the 12 complete turns.

The solid navy orbit shows the selected revolution and dashed orbits show neighboring turns. The arrow points in the direction of motion as time advances. The open diamond marks the once-per-revolution trigger, and the hollow circle shows the point linked to both waveforms.

At 0°, the selected point sits on the first trigger in the selected turn. At 360°, it reaches the next trigger. Between triggers, the chart assumes constant speed and linearly interpolates between adjacent probe samples.

The reported RPM is 60 times the sample rate divided by the number of samples between adjacent triggers. Keep the probe orientation and sign conventions consistent across runs to compare orbit shape and direction.

frequency-response.summary: Inspect one complex frequency response as Bode magnitude, Bode phase, and a Nyquist curve.
frequency-response.useWhen: Compare controller gains, locate resonant peaks, or relate the phase and magnitude at a frequency to the loop’s position in the complex plane.
frequency-response.data: Supply one or more responses, each with a unique ID and a label. Provide at least two positive, strictly increasing frequencies in Hz. The real and imaginary arrays must have the same length as the frequency array, with a finite, nonzero complex magnitude at every sample.
frequency-response.reading: Choose a loop gain and select a frequency in a panel or with the Frequency control. Open circles identify the same sample in all three panels. The framed Bode panels align their logarithmic frequency ticks in Hz, with horizontal reference guides at 0 dB for magnitude and −180° for phase.
notes: The simulated loop combines a 28 Hz second-order elastic mode with damping ratio 0.14 and a first-order lag with a 45 Hz corner frequency. The example plots the modeled open-loop response at 301 sampled frequencies from 0.6 to 200 Hz for gains of 0.48 and 0.84.

The chart takes magnitude in decibels as 20 × log₁₀ of the complex modulus and phase as the signed angle in degrees. Phase unwrapping assumes the true phase changes by less than 180° between adjacent samples.

The white Nyquist panel uses equal scales for the horizontal real axis and the vertical imaginary axis. The solid curve joins the positive-frequency samples. For real-coefficient systems, the dashed negative-frequency branch is their complex conjugate reflected across the real axis.

The cross at (−1, 0) marks where 1 + L equals zero under unity negative feedback. Near 33.7 Hz the modeled nominal response crosses the real axis at about −0.68 and the higher-gain response crosses at about −1.20. The chart covers the sampled frequency band. A stability analysis needs the full Nyquist contour and the count of open-loop poles in the right half-plane.

coherence-phase.summary: Read magnitude-squared coherence and signed cross-phase at the same frequency.
coherence-phase.useWhen: Check which frequency components two sensors share and whether their relative phase is consistent over a test run.
coherence-phase.data: Supply spectral estimates from synchronized sensor recordings. For each run, provide a unique ID and label, at least two nonnegative frequencies in Hz in strictly increasing order, and aligned arrays of finite coherence and phase values. Coherence ranges from 0 to 1. Wrap phase to the −180° to 180° interval.
coherence-phase.reading: Choose a Recording, then select a frequency in either panel or with the Frequency control. A shared cursor identifies the same bin in the coherence and phase panels. Frequency band can restrict the view to the lower quarter of the range when that interval contains at least two bins.
notes: The example compares the first baseline and drive-end unbalance recordings at a nominal 30 Hz shaft speed (1,800 RPM) on the same Universidade de São Paulo rig. The source files are Normal_30Hz_001.lvm and Desbalanc1_30Hz_001.lvm. The unbalance recording lists an added 18.13 g mass at 0°.

Channel X is horizontal acceleration at the drive-end bearing and channel Y is horizontal acceleration at the non-drive-end bearing. Each six-second record contains 36,000 synchronized samples per channel at 6,000 Hz.

The displayed estimates use 34 Welch segments with per-segment mean removal, a 2,048-sample periodic Hann window, and 1,024 samples of overlap. The 512 displayed frequency bins span about 2.93–1,500 Hz with 2.93 Hz spacing. The preview starts on the bin nearest the nominal shaft speed, at 29.30 Hz.

Estimate the auto-spectra Pxx and Pyy and cross-spectrum Pxy with the same Welch window, segment length, overlap, and sampling rate. Magnitude-squared coherence is |Pxy|²/(Pxx Pyy). Values near 1 indicate a consistent linear association at that frequency.

The phase convention is Y relative to X. Phase is arg(Pxy), where the Welch cross-spectrum averages segment products conj(X)Y. Swapping X and Y reverses the phase sign. A pure delay τ from X to Y gives phase −360° × frequency × τ modulo 360°, with time in seconds.

Coherence threshold starts at 0.60 and controls the phase display. Phase has gaps at bins below the selected cutoff and at jumps across the ±180° wrap. Interpreting phase or choosing a statistical threshold requires knowledge of the sensor setup and the spectral estimates.

wavelet-scalogram.summary: Locate short vibration events and changing frequencies, then inspect the waveform at the same time.
wavelet-scalogram.useWhen: Analyze a signal whose frequency content changes over time, such as during a machine run-up or a short vibration burst.
wavelet-scalogram.data: Supply strictly increasing times in seconds, strictly increasing positive frequencies in Hz, and a matrix of finite relative power values in dB. Index the matrix as powerDb[frequencyIndex][timeIndex]. Provide the matching waveform with startSeconds, a positive sampleRateHz, a unit label, and uniformly sampled finite values.
wavelet-scalogram.reading: The scalogram plots time horizontally and frequency on a logarithmic vertical axis. The colorbar shows wavelet power relative to the peak. Select a time and frequency in the map or with the controls, then inspect the linked waveform and adjust its time window.
notes: The example uses Channel_1 of the measured University of Ottawa I-A-1 inner-race fault run-up. The full 200 kHz recording is low-pass filtered with a Kaiser window (β = 5) and resampled to 12.5 kHz before extracting 3.500–6.060 s. The linked waveform shows the demeaned segment in multiples of its root-mean-square amplitude.

The transform uses zero-padded convolution with a sampled unit-energy complex Morlet wavelet (ω₀ = 6). The map contains 100 log-spaced equivalent Fourier frequencies from 30 to 3,000 Hz and 640 four-millisecond time bins. Each cell retains the maximum wavelet power in its time bin.

For transform coefficients W, compute power P = |W|² and report 10 × log₁₀(P/Pₘₐₓ). The strongest retained cell in this map sets 0 dB, and the display floor is −60 dB. Keep the wavelet, scaling, and reference consistent when comparing levels.

The cone-of-influence boundaries mark where finite-record edges can affect the estimates. coiEdgeSeconds supplies one inward time margin per frequency row, set to √2 times the Morlet scale in this example. Lower-frequency wavelets extend farther in time.

bearing-envelope.summary: Select a carrier band and inspect the corresponding vibration envelope in shaft orders.
bearing-envelope.useWhen: Explore repeated amplitude modulation in accelerometer recordings, or compare how different carrier bands reveal different repetition rates as a shaft speeds up.
bearing-envelope.data: Supply shared, strictly increasing frequency bins in Hz and shaft-order bins. Define each band with a unique id, a label, and its lower and upper limits in Hz. Each recording supplies a broadbandDb array aligned to frequencyHz and one envelope array aligned to orders per band id. Supply finite relative levels in dB with a common reference for each panel across recordings and bands.
bearing-envelope.reading: Choose a bearing recording and a carrier band. The broadband panel highlights that band in Hz and the envelope panel shows modulation in cycles per shaft revolution. Select an order to read its level. Relative dB scales stay fixed while you compare bands and recordings.
notes: The University of Ottawa example compares the healthy H-A-1 and inner-race fault I-A-1 run-ups. Channel_1 acceleration is low-pass filtered with a Kaiser window (β = 5) and resampled from 200 kHz to 20 kHz. Each analysis uses 60 measured shaft turns starting at the first 2 V rising crossing of the Channel_2 encoder signal after 3.000 s.

The broadband panel estimates power spectral density with Welch averaging, using 1,024-sample periodic Hann windows, 512 samples of overlap, and removal of each segment mean. It shows 409 positive bins from about 19.53 to 7,988.28 Hz. Carrier bands are 800–1,600, 1,600–3,200, and 3,200–6,400 Hz.

For each carrier band, apply a forward–reverse Butterworth band-pass filter with order parameter 4 and take the magnitude of the Hilbert analytic signal. A forward–reverse 450 Hz low-pass filter with order parameter 8 limits the envelope before interpolation onto every eighth encoder pulse, giving 128 samples per shaft revolution.

The envelope order spectrum uses the demeaned signal with a periodic Hann window and amplitude correction for window gain. The display contains 900 positive bins from 1/60 to 15 shaft orders. The broadband level is 10 × log₁₀ of the ratio to the shared peak power spectral density. The envelope level is 20 × log₁₀ of the ratio to the shared peak amplitude across runs and bands. Both displays have a −65 dB floor.

The ER16K bearing geometry gives expected ball-pass references at 3.57 orders for the outer race (BPFO) and 5.43 orders for the inner race (BPFI), with the second BPFI harmonic at 10.86 orders. The example opens on the inner-race recording in the 3,200–6,400 Hz carrier band at 5.45 orders. These guides are geometric predictions, and interpretation depends on the operating conditions, slip, and sensor response.

eye-diagram.summary: Overlay symbol intervals to compare voltage margin, crossing jitter, and overshoot in a binary signal.
eye-diagram.useWhen: Explore where to sample an NRZ signal or compare how channel impairments affect the eye opening.
eye-diagram.data: Supply strictly increasing time samples in unit intervals (UI), spanning at least 0 to 1 UI, and a positive symbol rate in baud. Each run supplies a unique id, a label, nominal low and high voltage levels in mV, and folded traces whose voltages align to timeUi. For each trace, previousBit labels the bit before 0 UI and bit labels the bit in the central interval.
eye-diagram.reading: Choose a Channel and use Sampling phase to move the sampling line through the central symbol interval. The eye height updates at the selected phase, which starts at 0.5 UI. The crossing bracket spans the fifth to 95th percentiles of crossing times near the leading symbol boundary.
notes: Each channel simulates one full 127-symbol PRBS7 period at 1 Gbaud with nominal levels of −400 and 400 mV. The 127 folds span −0.5 to 1.5 UI at 64 samples per UI against an ideal clock. At this symbol rate, 1 UI is 1,000 ps.

The reference channel uses a critically damped second-order response. The impaired channel has lower damping, with 24% of the response delayed by 0.58 UI, larger timing offsets, and more voltage noise. Both channels use periodic and seeded random timing offsets.

At the selected phase the chart linearly interpolates each trace between sampled voltages. Eye height is the fifth percentile of high-bit voltages minus the 95th percentile of low-bit voltages. A negative height means the two percentile bounds overlap.

Crossing jitter uses traces with a bit change. For each trace, use the same-direction crossing of the nominal rail midpoint closest to 0 UI within ±0.35 UI, found by linear interpolation. Include only traces with a crossing in that window. RMS jitter is the population root mean square of those crossing times after subtracting their mean, converted to picoseconds using the symbol rate.
Overshoot reports the greatest excursion above the high rail or below the low rail across the folded traces, as a percentage of the nominal full swing. The lower-rail excursion is undershoot.
At 0.5 UI the reference and impaired eye heights are about 795 and 364 mV, respectively. The simulations give about 3.5 and 39.6 ps RMS crossing jitter and 0.49% and 8.51% overshoot.

allan-deviation.summary: Compare the stability of a measured quantity across different averaging times.
allan-deviation.useWhen: Inspect clock frequency or inertial-sensor noise over short and long averaging intervals.
allan-deviation.data: Supply the name of the measured quantity and its unit if applicable. Give each curve a unique ID, a label, and points ordered by strictly increasing averaging time. Each point needs a positive finite tauSeconds and deviation for the logarithmic axes. Add pairs when the number of contributing overlapping terms is available.
allan-deviation.reading: The horizontal axis is averaging time τ in seconds and the vertical axis is Allan deviation in the quantity’s units. Both axes are logarithmic. Choose a Recording, then use Averaging time or the plot to read deviation and the overlapping pair count when supplied. Lower deviation indicates more stable averages at that timescale.
notes: The example uses 44,002 synchronized phase samples, one second apart, from the NIST optical-clock and 10 GHz microwave comparison. Convert recorded phase φ in radians to time error x = φ/(2πν), using the experiment’s 259 THz optical reference and 10 GHz microwave reference. Convert the recorded microwave values from milliradians first.

The difference curve uses the sample-by-sample microwave time error minus optical time error. It describes the paired recordings, both of which compare two devices. Nakamura et al. report their separate optical-to-microwave transfer measurement in the paper.

Overlapping Allan deviation compares adjacent averages of duration τ. Start successive pairs one sample apart. For this one-second time-error data, τ = m seconds and each contributing value is (x[i + 2m] − 2x[i + m] + x[i])/τ. The deviation is the square root of one half the mean square of the N − 2m terms. The example spans 1–10,000 s.

At τ = 100 s the optical and microwave deviations are about 2.86 × 10⁻¹⁷ and 2.87 × 10⁻¹⁷. Their matched-record difference has deviation 3.45 × 10⁻¹⁸. Each estimate uses 43,802 overlapping terms, which share input samples. Confidence intervals depend on the effective degrees of freedom, the noise process, and the averaging factor.

Show reference slopes adds ideal power-law guides on the log–log plot. White frequency modulation (FM) has slope −½, flicker FM has slope 0, and random-walk FM has slope +½. Compare the surrounding points and the record length when interpreting a measured slope.

phase-plane.summary: Follow position and velocity together, with the selected state linked to its time in the trajectory.
phase-plane.useWhen: Inspect how an oscillator approaches equilibrium, compare trajectories under different damping, or examine the direction of motion in state space.
phase-plane.data: Supply labels and units for the position and velocity axes. Give each trajectory a unique ID, a label, and samples with strictly increasing timeSeconds and finite position and velocity values. For a continuous rotation, supply an unwrapped angular position coordinate.
phase-plane.reading: Choose a Trajectory and move the Time control or select a point on the linked position history. The main plot shows position horizontally and velocity vertically, with an arrow pointing in the direction of increasing time. The markers identify the same recorded state in both views.
notes: The example uses three recordings of the same 0.607 m pendulum from the Damped Pendulum Dataset. The damping setups are air only, a small paper baffle, and a large paper baffle. The PASCO PS-3220 recordings report angle in radians and angular velocity in radians per second at 100 Hz.

The excerpts use trials len5_cond1_2, len5_cond2_2, and len5_cond3_1. Time starts at the last recorded zero-velocity sample before the sustained inward swing. Starting angles are 0.553, 0.603, and 0.559 rad. The chart retains every fourth sample through 16 s, for 401 displayed samples per trajectory at 25 Hz.
For an undriven pendulum, the hanging state at zero angle and zero angular velocity is an equilibrium. With dissipation, the measured loops contract as the motion approaches that state.

The copyable oscillator example supplies a model for the direction field. Pass acceleration(position, velocity) to draw the rate vector (velocity, acceleration) at each state. Use consistent units, with velocity equal to position units per second and acceleration equal to velocity units per second. Show direction field toggles the model arrows when valid acceleration values are available.

xrd-peak-tracker.summary: Inspect a diffraction peak fit and follow its center, width, and height across temperatures.
xrd-peak-tracker.useWhen: Compare how an observed feature shifts, broadens, or changes height in temperature-resolved diffraction scans.
xrd-peak-tracker.data: Supply a shared, strictly increasing angleDeg axis in degrees 2θ. Provide scans in increasing temperature order in kelvin, with one finite intensity value per angle. Give each peak a unique ID, a label, a fixed window in degrees 2θ, and one fit per scan in the same order. Use null when a fit is unavailable.
xrd-peak-tracker.reading: Choose a Peak and move the Temperature control. The profile shows measured sample markers, a fitted curve over the fixed window, and its linear background. The bracket marks the full width at half maximum (FWHM). Three aligned temperature plots follow the fitted center, FWHM, and peak height above background.
notes: The example uses 16 measured DyNiC₂ synchrotron X-ray diffraction scans from 10.91 to 294.11 K. The scans share 163 samples from about 5.002 to 5.500° 2θ. The fixed windows are 5.157–5.247°, 5.252–5.322°, and 5.324–5.407° and identify observed features by angle.

Bounded, unweighted least squares fits a pseudo-Voigt peak, a Gaussian–Lorentzian mixture with a shared center and width, plus a linear background. The background intercept is defined at the fitted center. Height is the fitted peak contribution above that background, in arbitrary intensity units (a.u.). FWHM measures the separation of the points at half that height above the local background.

The fit tries starting Lorentzian fractions of 0.1, 0.5, and 0.9. Among converged solutions with finite parameters and center, width, and height away from their bounds, it selects the smallest sum of squared intensity residuals. The example retains all 48 fits. An unavailable fit appears as a gap in the temperature trends.

For the feature near 5.36°, the fitted center changes from 5.36450° at 10.91 K to 5.34403° at 294.11 K. The fitted width changes from 0.01875° to 0.02561°. Inspect the measured markers, fitted curve, and root-mean-square intensity residual to assess each local fit.

stress-strain-comparison.summary: Compare tensile curves on shared engineering axes and inspect the 0.2% proof-stress construction.
stress-strain-comparison.useWhen: Compare recorded tensile responses across heat treatments or inspect how an elastic fit defines an offset proof stress.
stress-strain-comparison.data: Give each curve a unique ID, a label, and finite engineering stress in MPa at strictly increasing engineering strain. Supply strain as a fraction, so 0.002 represents 0.2%. Provide the elastic-fit strain bounds, slope in MPa, and stress intercept in MPa. A zero-based fractureIndex ends the curve at a documented break point.
stress-strain-comparison.reading: Choose a Condition. The main panel overlays the recorded curves. The detail panel shows the selected curve at low strain, its fitted elastic line, and the parallel line shifted by 0.2% strain. The proof-stress marker sits where the offset line intersects the curve.
notes: The example compares measured EN AW-2618A tensile curves for the T61 reference (ABR5RTzl1) and after 15,000 h of additional ageing at 160 °C (ABR10RTzl1) or 190 °C (ABR8RTzl1). Each test used a DIN 50125 B6 × 30 specimen at 20 °C and a nominal strain rate of 0.0001 s⁻¹ under ISO 6892-1.

Engineering strain uses the original gauge length and engineering stress divides force by the original cross-sectional area. The figure retains measured points at successive new highs in strain, then selects points by strain bin while preserving the proof-stress bracket, tensile maximum, and last retained point.

The modulus estimate E is the slope of the elastic fit Eε + b. The example uses ordinary least squares on 0.05–0.15% strain for all three curves. The offset line is E(ε − 0.002) + b. The chart interpolates the first crossing of that line after the fit interval where the curve moves from above to below it.

The calculated 0.2% proof stresses are about 363, 283, and 249 MPa for T61, 160 °C ageing, and 190 °C ageing, respectively. The corresponding recorded tensile maxima are 428.7, 362.0, and 342.8 MPa. Each endpoint represents the last retained stress–strain sample.

full-field-strain.summary: Inspect where surface strain localizes during loading and read the force at the selected stage.
full-field-strain.useWhen: Compare spatial strain maps across a tensile experiment or link a highly strained region to the specimen’s load history.
full-field-strain.data: Supply shared, strictly increasing xMm and yMm axes. Order frames by stage and give each frame a force in newtons and one strain value in percent per grid site. Order values by y row with x varying fastest. Use null for unavailable samples. Provide a fixed strainDomainPercent and use the same stage coordinates and units in optional forceHistory.
full-field-strain.reading: Use Frame or select a point on the load history to change the displayed map. Click or tap the field to inspect a grid site. With the field focused, use the arrow keys to move between sites. The point readout gives the original supplied grid value and coordinates.
notes: The example uses the measured TPS_2 digital image correlation test on a T-shaped polyurethane specimen under tensile loading. The map uses undeformed specimen coordinates, with x increasing to the right and y upward. The conversion uses the study’s 21 µm per pixel calibration.

The chart shows Green–Lagrange strain Eyy derived from measured horizontal and vertical displacements u and v. A centered linear fit over five valid native samples estimates their vertical gradients. Eyy = ((∂u/∂y)² + (1 + ∂v/∂y)² − 1)/2, expressed in percent.

The 14 maps retain every fifth grid site on each axis, yielding a 39 × 58 lattice at 0.525 mm spacing with 1,189 valid sites per map. The load history uses all 63 loaded frames from 1.0 to 62.9 s. The force rows in force_vfm.csv match the HDF5 loaded frames in order, and elapsed time comes from the frame metadata.

The colorbar stays fixed at −5% to 70% for this example. Color values beyond the scale use its endpoint colors. The map interpolates colors between four valid neighbors and uses the nearest site in partially masked cells, leaving unavailable sites blank. The probe reads the stored value, rounded in this example to 0.001 percentage point.
At x = 12.075 mm and y = 23.100 mm, the strain is 40.316% at 45 s under 49.667 N. At 62.9 s it reaches 67.033% under 58.394 N at the same reference coordinate.

fatigue-sn.summary: Plot stress amplitude against cycles to failure or test stop, using measured 42CrMo4+QT steel data from the FABEST benchmark.
fatigue-sn.useWhen: Inspect specimen-level stress–life data, including the spread in test outcomes at similar stress levels.
fatigue-sn.data: Supply one or more nonempty series with unique series IDs. Within each series, each test needs a unique specimen ID, a finite positive stress in MPa, a positive safe integer for cycles, and outcome failure or runout. Set stressLabel to identify the stress measure and stressRatio when the source reports it.
fatigue-sn.reading: Cycles are on a logarithmic horizontal axis and stress in MPa is on a linear vertical axis. Use Outcome to filter the plot. Select a mark or use Specimen to read its observation. For multiple campaigns, Series selects a group of tests. The axes keep the same scale as you filter.
notes: Each plotted point is one specimen test. Failure records the cycle count at the study’s failure criterion. A right-facing arrow marks a run-out, meaning the specimen reached the plotted cycle count before the test stopped. Its lifetime is right-censored at that count.

Stress amplitude is half the difference between maximum and minimum stress in one cycle. Stress ratio R is minimum stress divided by maximum stress. Use comparable definitions and loading conditions when comparing series.

The example plots 22 measured tests from the FABEST v4 workbook (CC BY 4.0). Setups 37 and 35 used hollow, unnotched steel specimens under constant-amplitude axial tension–compression at R = −1. The vertical axis shows nominal stress amplitude on the net section.

FABEST records complete break as failure for these tests. Setup 37 has 10 failures and two interrupted tests. Setup 35 has 10 failures. Select specimen FAB060_A37-02B to see a complete break at 11,893 cycles and 800 MPa. The two 600 MPa run-outs in Setup 37 stopped at 2,634,775 and 13,149,279 cycles, giving separate lower bounds on their lives.
The figure shows individual observations and their censoring. To estimate a stress–life curve, use a model that accounts for right-censoring and the test conditions.

crack-growth.summary: Explore how fatigue crack-growth rate changes with stress-intensity range in measured compact-tension tests on three high-strength steels.
crack-growth.useWhen: Compare fatigue crack growth across material or test series and estimate a Paris-law exponent over a selected range of measured values.
crack-growth.data: Give each series a unique ID and at least three points ordered by increasing or equal deltaK. Both deltaK in MPa√m and rateMmPerCycle in mm/cycle must be finite and positive. Supply stressRatio when available. Optional fitRange sets the initial ΔK bounds and needs at least three points spanning two distinct ΔK values. Otherwise the chart starts with the full series.
crack-growth.reading: Both axes are logarithmic. The horizontal axis is stress-intensity factor range ΔK, in MPa√m. The vertical axis is crack advance per cycle da/dN, in mm/cycle. Use Series to switch curves when multiple are available. Click a marker or use Measurement to read its values. Set Fit from and Fit through to change which points are included in the fit. Filled markers are included and open markers are outside the fit interval.
notes: In the Paris law da/dN = C(ΔK)ᵐ, m is the slope of log₁₀(da/dN) against log₁₀(ΔK) and log₁₀(C) is the intercept. The chart estimates both by ordinary least squares on the selected points and reports R² in log space with the count of those points.
C uses units of (mm/cycle)/(MPa√m)ᵐ. Compare coefficients after matching the units and accounting for the specimen, loading conditions, and fitted interval.
Select the approximately linear part of the log–log curve for a Paris-law fit. The line spans the selected observations. Threshold and rapid fracture regions may follow different relationships.

The example compares S460, S690, and S960 compact-tension curves from Seitl et al. The specimens had the same effective width (50 mm) and thickness (10 mm) and were tested at 22 ± 1 °C in opening mode (mode I), with a force ratio of R = 0.1. The study estimated crack length from the compliance of clip-gauge measurements of crack mouth opening displacement (CMOD).

The example groups points by steel grade and uses the positive ΔK and da/dN pairs from the workbook’s selected CMOD columns. The plotted values retain their published units. Each grade starts with the common 10–20 MPa√m fit interval. The displayed coefficients depend on the measurements that fall inside that interval.
For S460, the default interval includes 12 observations and gives m ≈ 2.985 and log-space R² ≈ 0.998. Select the S460 point near ΔK = 13.50 MPa√m to read a growth rate of 9.673 × 10⁻⁶ mm/cycle.

binary-phase-diagram.summary: Explore how the equilibrium phases of a two-component material change with composition and temperature.
binary-phase-diagram.useWhen: Read liquidus, solidus, and solvus boundaries, follow a fixed-composition cooling path, and calculate fractions in a two-phase field.
binary-phase-diagram.data: Provide two distinct component names, the composition unit (at. % or wt. % of the second component), a temperature domain in °C, a eutectic temperature and three compositions, and six boundary branches. Each branch needs at least two samples with composition from 0 to 100 and strictly increasing temperatures within the display domain. On each side, join the liquidus and solidus at the corresponding pure-component melting point. Each solvus spans the display minimum to the eutectic. Match every branch at the eutectic temperature to its corresponding eutectic composition.
binary-phase-diagram.reading: The horizontal axis gives the overall percentage of the second component and the vertical axis gives temperature. Click or drag the point on the figure, or use Composition and Temperature. Follow the vertical path to see which fields the alloy enters on cooling. In a two-phase field, the ends of the horizontal tie line show the compositions of the two phases. Use Go to eutectic to select the exact invariant temperature and liquid composition.
notes: The liquidus separates fully liquid material from liquid plus solid. The solidus marks the limit of fully solid material. A solvus marks the composition limit of a solid solution.

For a bulk composition x₀ between tie-line endpoints xₗ and xᵣ, the fraction of the left phase is (xᵣ − x₀)/(xᵣ − xₗ) and the fraction of the right phase is (x₀ − xₗ)/(xᵣ − xₗ). With atomic percent these are mole fractions on an atom basis. With weight percent they are mass fractions.

Between the solid endpoints of the invariant eutectic line, three equilibrium phase compositions are fixed. Bulk composition and temperature provide too little information to determine three phase fractions. The diagram represents equilibrium at the specified pressure. Rates of solidification and diffusion require a kinetic model.

The Ag–Cu example uses the Moon et al. thermodynamic assessment from Hallstedt’s SGTE collection. ORCHID calculated the equilibrium boundaries with pycalphad 0.11.2 at 1 atm. The figure converts kelvin to °C and Cu mole fraction to atomic percent. Tie-line endpoints are linearly interpolated from the published boundary samples.

The calculated eutectic is at 779.13 °C. The Ag-rich solid, liquid, and Cu-rich solid compositions there are 13.274, 40.254, and 95.460 at. % Cu. The separate NIST Ag–Cu calculation reports a liquid eutectic composition of 28.41 wt. % Cu using its own assessment.
At 20 at. % Cu and 850 °C, the Ag-rich solid contains about 9.08 at. % Cu and the liquid about 21.62 at. % Cu. The lever rule gives about 87.1% liquid on a mole basis.

ternary-mixture-map.summary: Compare observed three-component mixtures with a fitted response surface over the sampled composition range.
ternary-mixture-map.useWhen: Explore a mixture experiment in which three proportions share a common basis and sum to 100%.
ternary-mixture-map.data: Provide three component names ordered top, bottom left, bottom right. Each observation needs a unique ID, three fractions from 0 to 1 that sum to 1, and a finite response. Supply at least three non-collinear compositions, the response name and unit, fitted model coefficients, and a color domain in the response units. Use shortComponents to abbreviate names on the plot.
ternary-mixture-map.reading: In the full triangle each corner represents 100% of one component. Moving parallel to the opposite edge keeps that component’s proportion constant. For a narrow sampled range, the initial view zooms in using the smallest sampled proportion of each component and reports actual percentages. Select Show full composition triangle to see the full 0–100% axes. Click the triangle to inspect a composition. Click a marker or use Observation to compare measured and fitted responses. The first two composition controls determine the third fraction as the remaining percentage.
notes: The model uses fractions on the 0–1 scale. Pass coefficients in the order of terms [a, b, c, ab, ac, bc] for a Scheffé quadratic. Add the abc coefficient in the seventh slot for a special cubic. Estimate the coefficients from your data before passing them to the chart.

Color shows the fitted response, with contours tracing equal fitted values. The color and fitted readout are available inside the convex hull, the smallest convex region enclosing the sampled compositions. The hull describes the range of compositions. Prediction uncertainty is a separate estimate.

The example uses the ten binder compositions and mean uniaxial compressive strengths published by Xu et al. in Tables 2 and 3. The axes show mass percentages of three dry binder ingredients, ground granulated blast-furnace slag, fly ash, and red mud. The water-to-binder ratio and other constituents were fixed. Strength was measured on 50 mm by 100 mm cylinders after 28 days of curing.

The displayed Scheffé quadratic is an unweighted least-squares fit to the ten reported means. Its in-sample RMSE is 2.48 MPa. In leave-one-out cross-validation on these ten mixtures, adding the special cubic term increased RMSE from 10.73 to 13.06 MPa.
Select G30F60R10 to compare the measured mean of 89.0 MPa with the fitted value of 85.92 MPa at 30% slag, 60% fly ash, and 10% red mud.

industrial-ct.summary: Inspect the same industrial X-ray CT volume in three linked cross-sections and a rotatable view of segmented pores.
industrial-ct.useWhen: Locate pore features in a scan, examine their shape from multiple angles, or inspect their volume at known voxel spacing.
industrial-ct.data: Supply dimensions and positive voxel spacing in X, Y, Z order, with at least two voxels on each axis. The gray and labels arrays must each contain nx × ny × nz entries. Store X fastest at x + nx × (y + ny × z). Gray is an 8-bit display volume. Label 0 is unassigned and each positive label identifies a pore. Set originMm to the physical coordinates of voxel (0, 0, 0) if the crop has an offset.
industrial-ct.reading: Axial (XY) holds Z fixed, coronal (XZ) holds Y fixed, and sagittal (YZ) holds X fixed. Click a slice or use X slice, Y slice, and Z slice to move their shared intersection. Select a pore from Pore or pick it on the 3D reconstruction. Drag to turn the 3D view, or use Rotate left and Rotate right. Use Show pore mask to display the segmentation over the slices.
notes: The three planes are cross-sections of the same grayscale and label volumes. A crosshair shows the shared voxel position. Its physical coordinates are the crop origin plus the voxel indices multiplied by the corresponding spacing.

Pore volume is the number of voxels carrying the pore’s label multiplied by the volume per voxel. The 3D reconstruction draws the exposed faces of the labeled voxels at the supplied physical scale. Selecting a pore centers the crosshairs on its labeled voxel nearest the centroid.

Grayscale values report display intensity on a 0–255 scale. Physical density and attenuation require additional scanner calibration. Pore size and shape estimates depend on voxel resolution and the supplied segmentation.

The measured example crops a 64 × 64 × 64 volume from NIST’s set 1, sample 2. The scan is of laser powder bed–fused cobalt–chromium and the voxel pitch is 2.45 µm along each axis. The crop starts at source voxel (362, 518, 372), with reconstructed slices 0372–0435 in increasing order.
All three views use the same display window. The example clips the source 16-bit intensities to 34,000–57,000 and maps that range linearly to 0–255, rounding to whole numbers.

The example takes pore voxels from the published binary mask. It labels face-connected pore regions, keeping those with at least 25 voxels that lie fully inside the crop, then orders them by volume. The four volumes describe these retained regions within the crop.
Select Pore 1 to inspect 959 labeled voxels, a volume of 1.4103 × 10⁻⁵ mm³. The shared probe moves to local voxel (25, 12, 37), where Display intensity reads 47 / 255.

cad-scan-deviation.summary: Inspect signed distances between a registered 3D scan and a nominal CAD surface, with a linked section through the part.
cad-scan-deviation.useWhen: Compare a measured surface with its nominal reference and locate points beyond a specified deviation band.
cad-scan-deviation.data: Provide the nominal surface as finite XYZ vertices and nondegenerate triangles with zero-based vertex indices. For each scan point, supply its position, its closest point on the nominal surface, and signed deviation in millimeters. Register both surfaces in one physical coordinate frame before passing the data. Optionally set sectionAxis, a positive colorLimitMm, and a nonnegative toleranceMm.
cad-scan-deviation.reading: Drag the 3D view or use Rotate left and Rotate right. With focus on the 3D view, press Up or Down to change the tilt. Select a measured point in either view to inspect its signed deviation and bring the section through that point. With focus on the section, press Left or Right to select a nearby measured point. Use Show nominal surface to control the 3D reference overlay. Move Section position to intersect the nominal mesh with a plane and see nearby scan points projected onto it. Use Tolerance (mm) to set the symmetric deviation band and Outside tolerance only to filter the measured points.
notes: The distance magnitude is the Euclidean distance to the nearest point on the nominal surface. The sign follows the orientation of the nearest reference face. A positive deviation is on the normal-facing side. A negative deviation is on the opposite side. Use consistent reference normals when computing signed distances.

The color bar gives signed deviations in millimeters. Blue marks negative deviations and red marks positive deviations. Values beyond the endpoints use the endpoint colors and keep their numerical deviation. Tolerance is applied to the absolute deviation before rounding the readout. The section projects samples from a slab around the plane and retains their supplied 3D deviations.

The viewer uses the supplied alignment and point-to-surface distances. Document the frame, registration method, and reference orientation alongside your data. The tolerance control applies a band to the supplied points. A part-level conformance decision also depends on its tolerance specification, scan coverage, and measurement uncertainty.

The example compares measured Part 4 from the NIST Overhang Part X4 study with its nominal 9 mm × 5 mm × 5 mm CAD geometry. The part was printed in nickel superalloy 625 with a 45° overhang and a horizontal cylindrical cutout. NIST measured the part with X-ray CT at 11.95 µm isotropic voxel pitch and published the cleaned surface mesh.

The study established a 3-2-1 datum frame from the base cut by electrical discharge machining, the long side, and one end face. The example refines that alignment with a rigid fit to the same datum surfaces. The machining step removed some material from the base after printing.

To sample the measured mesh, the example takes vertices from every 32nd triangle and keeps a representative nearest the center of each occupied 0.32 mm bin. Distances for the resulting 3,601 locations use all 2,904 triangles of the original nominal mesh. The viewer uses a lighter 1,464-triangle mesh to draw the nominal surface.

At the example’s ±0.10 mm tolerance, 1,269 of the 3,601 sampled locations are outside the band. The color bar spans ±0.60 mm. The initial point at about (1.063, 2.421, 3.453) mm lies inside the nominal bore with a positive deviation of 1.044 mm. Its color reaches the endpoint while the readout retains its value. The XZ section starts at the selected point’s Y coordinate and shows samples within 0.089 mm on either side.

cie-chromaticity.summary: Compare display gamuts and probe chromaticity in two coordinate systems using the CIE 1931 standard observer.
cie-chromaticity.useWhen: Compare standardized or measured display primaries, check whether a chromaticity lies within a gamut, or quantify how much of a reference gamut a second gamut covers.
cie-chromaticity.data: Supply at least three spectral-locus samples in increasing wavelength order, each with a wavelength in nanometers and its CIE 1931 xy coordinates. Give each gamut a unique ID, a label, and at least three non-collinear primaries in xy. The chart uses their convex hull. An optional white point must lie within its gamut. Supply initialPoint and initialGamuts to set the starting probe and comparison.
cie-chromaticity.reading: Use Coordinate space to switch between CIE 1931 xy and CIE 1976 u′v′. Choose Reference gamut and Comparison gamut to set the two regions. Click within the diagram’s visible chromaticity boundary to probe a point. With the plot focused, use the arrow keys to move by 0.005 in the active coordinates, or hold Shift to move by 0.025. The example starts at D65 and reports whether the probe lies in each gamut.
notes: The spectral locus is the curved boundary of monochromatic stimuli for the CIE 1931 2° standard observer. The straight line of purples joins its endpoints and describes mixtures of long- and short-wavelength light.
For CIE 1976 u′v′, let D = 3 − 2x + 12y. Then u′ = 4x/D and v′ = 9y/D. Switching spaces changes the plotted coordinates of the same chromaticity.

Coverage is the area common to both gamut polygons divided by the area of the reference polygon in the selected coordinate space. The comparison percentage uses the comparison polygon as the denominator. Switching coordinate spaces can change both percentages. This is a two-dimensional chromaticity area. Assessing color volume also requires a brightness or lightness dimension.

The example uses 471 published CIE locus samples from 360 to 830 nm in 1 nm steps. The three standardized gamuts are sRGB, Display P3, and Rec. 2020 (ITU-R BT.2020). Their D65 white point is (0.3127, 0.3290) in xy and approximately (0.19783, 0.46832) in u′v′.

Set Display P3 as Reference gamut and sRGB as Comparison gamut to see about 73.72% coverage in xy and 79.64% in u′v′. With the two gamuts reversed, Display P3 covers 100% of sRGB in both coordinate spaces. With Display P3 as the reference and Rec. 2020 as the comparison, coverage rounds to 99.98% in both spaces.
The diagram’s background uses illustrative sRGB colors. Use the locus, gamut boundaries, and coordinate readout for comparison.

hyperspectral-cube.useWhen: Explore which wavelengths distinguish spatial features in imaging spectroscopy data, or compare spectral variation within a region.
hyperspectral-cube.data: Supply positive integer dimensions, strictly increasing positive wavelengths in nanometers, and exactly width × height × band count values. Store each band as a complete image, with the column changing fastest. The flat index is b × width × height + y × width + x. Use noDataValue for a raw-value sentinel and excludedBands for zero-based band indices. Keep at least two bands available for inspection.
hyperspectral-cube.reading: Under Image mode, choose Single band for a grayscale image or RGB composite to assign wavelengths with Red band, Green band, and Blue band. Click or tap the image to inspect one pixel, or drag a rectangle to read a region spectrum. With the image focused, use arrow keys to pick a pixel or hold Shift to extend the region from its anchor. Pick a wavelength on the spectrum or use Wavelength band to switch the image to that band. With the spectrum focused, Left and Right step between bands. Home and End jump to the first and last available bands.
notes: Each valid sample is displayed as raw × valueScale + valueOffset. Source column and Source row are columnOrigin + x × pixelStride and rowOrigin + y × pixelStride. The initialPixel indexes the local cube. Use zero-based band indices for initialBand and for rgbBands ordered red, green, blue. A common display range keeps the image contrast scale fixed across wavelengths and RGB channels.

The region spectrum plots the mean of valid pixels at each wavelength. Across adjacent bands with two or more valid pixels, the envelope extends one population standard deviation above and below the mean. A band’s valid count can vary because no-data pixels are excluded separately at each wavelength.

Excluded bands and bands with zero valid pixels break the spectrum. RGB composite colors reflect the chosen channel wavelengths and the display range. Assigning infrared bands produces a false-color image. Use the spectral readout for numerical comparison.

The measured example uses NASA/JPL AVIRIS data acquired over Cuprite, Nevada, on June 23, 1995. The published cube is radiative transfer ground calibrated (RTGC). A stored value of 20,000 represents 100% reflectance, so each integer step is 0.005 percentage point. The archive uses −32,767 for deleted samples.

The 108 × 84 crop starts at zero-based source column 161 and row 409 and keeps every third source pixel along each axis. It retains 126 original bands from 383.15 to 2508.20 nm in wavelength order, with denser sampling between 2050 and 2400 nm. Eight retained bands near the low-signal atmospheric water absorption regions around 1400 and 1900 nm are excluded from inspection.

The opening false-color composite assigns 2270.05, 2210.28, and 2090.47 nm to red, green, and blue, using a fixed 19–40% image display range. The starting pixel at source column 416 and row 526 has 29.12% reflectance at 2210.28 nm. The same pixel reads 34.085% at 2150.42 nm and 34.575% at 2260.10 nm.

Select source columns 404–416 and rows 511–526 to compare the starting pixel with its neighborhood. At 2210.28 nm the 30 sampled pixels give a mean of about 31.347% and a population standard deviation of 3.316 percentage points.

mass-spectrum.summary: Explore the invariant mass of 100,000 muon pairs recorded by CMS at CERN.
mass-spectrum.useWhen: View an event-count distribution across a wide mass range and compare regions near known particle resonances.
mass-spectrum.data: The example bins the published invariant mass column in 240 logarithmically spaced intervals from 2 to 110 GeV. Use getExample('mass-spectrum-cms') with ChartPreview to render the measured sample.
mass-spectrum.reading: The horizontal axis shows the invariant mass of each muon pair in GeV. The vertical axis shows events per bin. Both axes use logarithmic spacing. Select a bin to read its mass interval and event count.
notes: The reference regions mark known resonances near 3.1 GeV (J/ψ), 9–11 GeV (the Υ family), and 91 GeV (Z boson). Use the educational sample to explore the structures around these masses.
CMS selected 100,000 events with exactly two muons, including at least one high-quality global muon. The example includes every published event, with both opposite-sign and same-sign pairs.
The bin intervals widen in GeV as mass increases. Compare counts with the corresponding interval widths when interpreting peaks at different masses.

spectrum.summary: Find recurring frequencies in a measured signal.
spectrum.useWhen: Check for a periodic component or compare dominant frequencies in signals captured at regular intervals.
spectrum.data: Pass precomputed frequency bins as a Float64Array and one amplitude column of equal length per series. Give the frequency and amplitude units in the axis labels.
spectrum.reading: A peak shows a stronger periodic component. A peak at one cycle per year corresponds to an annual cycle.
notes: The example uses 480 monthly dry-air CO₂ measurements from NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory, from January 1980 through December 2019.
The example removes a linear trend and applies a periodic Hann window to the full record. It shows one-sided peak amplitude in ppm for frequencies from 0.025 to 4 cycles per year.
When comparing spectra, keep the sampling rate, window, and amplitude normalization consistent. This chart displays the frequency bins you provide.

spectrogram.summary: Follow Mauna Loa’s annual CO₂ cycle and its weaker harmonics over time.
spectrogram.useWhen: Find which frequencies persist across a measured record and which are stronger in particular periods.
spectrogram.data: Pass sorted time and frequency bin centers, the widths of those bins, and one amplitude per cell. Set valueLayout to match the order of the flattened array.
spectrogram.reading: Read window center years along the bottom and cycles per year along the vertical axis. Select a cell or cycle button to trace that frequency’s amplitude across windows.
notes: The chart uses 480 NOAA Mauna Loa monthly dry-air CO₂ measurements from January 1980 through December 2019. It shows one-sided peak amplitudes in 31 bins from 0.25 to 4 cycles per year after removing a linear trend and applying a periodic Hann window to each segment.
The 33 eight-year windows are centered from 1984 through 2016. Each starts one year after the previous window, so adjacent estimates share seven years of observations.

For smooth color, the heatmap interpolates between neighboring bin-center amplitudes before applying the shifted-log color scale, ln(1 + amplitude / 0.02 ppm). The legend is labeled in ppm. The trace and readout show the original bin amplitudes in ppm.
Across these windows, the annual cycle ranges from 2.777 to 3.120 ppm, the six-month cycle from 0.763 to 1.006 ppm, and the four-month cycle from 0.041 to 0.179 ppm.
For frequency-major values, the offset is frequencyIndex × timeBins.length + timeIndex. For time-major values, the offset is timeIndex × frequencyBins.length + frequencyIndex.

spectral-waterfall.summary: Compare spectra across measured time windows or experimental conditions in a linked 3D waterfall, heatmap, and selected spectrum.
spectral-waterfall.useWhen: Follow peak shifts or changes in intensity across an ordered series, such as the same material measured at different temperatures.
spectral-waterfall.data: Pass strictly increasing spectralBins and scanValues in their original units. Supply one intensity per scan and bin in scan-major order. Use NaN for a missing measurement.
spectral-waterfall.reading: Rotate the waterfall to see how peaks develop. Click a plotted point or use the Scan and Spectral bin controls to read the original value. The heatmap and selected spectrum follow the same scan and bin.
notes: The frequency example reuses the Mauna Loa spectrogram values from the NOAA monthly record. Each scan is a 96-month analysis window and the depth axis shows its center year.
The materials example includes 16 measured DyNiC₂ diffraction scans from 10.91 to 294.11 K. It keeps the reported intensity values in a 5–5.5° diffraction-angle window.
The displayed spacing follows the supplied coordinates. If input scans use different spectral grids, align them to a shared grid before supplying the matrix and document the alignment method.

correlation-matrix.summary: Compare the strength and direction of linear relationships across measured variables.
correlation-matrix.useWhen: Screen several pairs of quantitative measurements, then follow up with scatter plots and checks for confounding variables.
correlation-matrix.data: Pass variable keys and labels, one precomputed coefficient per cell in a square matrix, and optionally sample counts, missing counts, or a mask. Keep the variable order consistent with the matrix.
correlation-matrix.reading: Pearson r ranges from −1 to 1. The sign gives the direction of linear association and the absolute value gives its strength. Check the sample count before interpreting a cell.
notes: The Palmer Penguins example compares bill length, bill depth, flipper length, and body mass across 342 complete observations collected from 2007 through 2009. The example pools species. Group differences can drive a pooled coefficient, so inspect within-group associations separately.

The steel example uses all 1,941 records from UCI Steel Plates Faults. It computes pairwise Pearson coefficients across defect area, X perimeter, Y perimeter, and steel plate thickness in their recorded units.
Defect area and perimeter come from the same outline. Their strong positive associations help identify measurements that may carry similar information.
Use the same coefficient definition across cells. Record your missing-data policy and set minSampleCount when small pairs should be flagged.

process-control.summary: Review successive measurements against a process baseline and compare their distribution with specified bounds.
process-control.useWhen: Show an individuals control chart to inspect stability over observation order. Show a capability histogram to compare the distribution with engineering specifications.
process-control.data: For the individuals chart, pass ordered observations and a series of readings to TimeSeries, with precomputed control limits and rule markers in spcTracks. For the histogram, pass ordered bin edges and counts to Distribution, with optional specification and target markers.
process-control.reading: The individuals chart compares each measurement with a center line and control limits estimated from a baseline. The histogram shows counts per bin and how the readings sit relative to specification limits.
notes: The examples use 195 heat flow meter calibration factors collected by NIST. The source gives the observation order and leaves the calibration factor unit unspecified.

The individuals example fixes its center and control limits from the first 100 readings. Limits are the baseline mean plus or minus three times the mean moving range divided by 1.128. Observation 189 falls below the lower control limit in the follow-up portion.

The histogram counts the readings in 14 bins of width 0.01. It shows illustrative specification limits of 9.20 and 9.32 and a target of 9.26. Use approved engineering specifications and assess stability before calculating process capability.
